analysis.one_liner: Gives taxpayers and businesses a voluntary flat tax of 19% then 17%, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The Flat Tax Act was introduced in the House in February 2017 with one co-sponsor besides its author, was referred to two committees, and died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill lets any individual or business make a one-way election to leave the regular income tax and pay a flat rate instead: 19% for the first two years, then 17%. Individuals would pay that rate only on cash wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits, with a large standard deduction and no credits. Businesses would pay it on receipts minus inputs, wages, and retirement contributions. The bill also completely repeals the estate and gift taxes, which applies to everyone whether or not they elect the flat tax, and requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber for any future Congress to raise the flat rate or shrink the deductions.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income individuals whose money comes from investments would benefit most, because the flat tax base counts only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation — interest, dividends, and capital gains are simply not in the base, so a person living off investments could elect in and owe nothing. Large estates also gain, since the bill repeals the estate and gift taxes outright for deaths and gifts after 2017, a benefit that matters only to the biggest inheritances. Businesses gain a chance to swap corporate income tax for a 17% tax on cash flow after deducting inputs and wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: An individual electing the flat tax pays 19% for two years and 17% thereafter on taxable income defined only as cash wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, minus a standard deduction of $16,248 for a single filer, $20,739 for a head of household, and $32,496 for a joint return, plus $6,998 per dependent child [S3].

Interest, dividends, capital gains, and other investment income are not included in the individual flat tax base at all, so taxpayers whose income is mostly investment returns would owe nothing on that income if they elect in [S3].

Businesses electing in pay 19% then 17% on gross active income reduced by deductions for business inputs, wages, and retirement contributions, replacing the corporate income tax and the alternative minimum tax [S3].
The bill repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for decedents dying and transfers made after December 31, 2017 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would bear the cost, since electors pay a single low rate, investment income drops out of the individual tax base for electors, and the estate tax disappears entirely, meaning other taxpayers or future spending would absorb the lost revenue. Electing workers would also lose every tax credit, including the earned income tax credit and child tax credit, because the bill allows no credits for anyone who elects the flat tax. Tax-exempt employers and federal, state, and local governments would face a new 19% then 17% tax on the value of noncash benefits, such as health coverage, provided to their employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, tax-credit claimants, tax-exempt and government employers

drawbacks.text: The flat rate is regressive relative to current law for upper-income electors and removes all tax credits for electors, including the earned income tax credit and child credit, because the bill disallows every credit for persons who elect the flat tax [S3].

Because the individual base excludes investment income entirely, a household living on capital gains and dividends could elect the flat tax and pay nothing on that income, shifting the tax burden toward wage earners [S3].

The repeal of the estate tax benefits only the largest estates, since under the law in effect in 2017 the tax applied above roughly $5.5 million per person, and the repeal is not optional — it takes effect for all estates regardless of whether anyone elects the flat tax [S3].

The bill hard-wires itself against future change: any bill to raise the flat rate or cut the standard or business deductions requires a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate to even be considered [S3].
Independent tax analysts have generally estimated flat tax proposals of this type would substantially reduce federal revenue, leaving either higher deficits or the need for offsetting cuts or taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The voluntary design limits the damage — anyone who thinks the current code treats them better can stay in it. But the mandatory estate tax repeal is a large, permanent tax cut for the wealthiest few percent of estates, the election option invites high-income households with investment income to pay little or nothing, and the two-thirds supermajority rule would make it extremely hard for any future Congress to fix the rate or restore the estate tax. The bill's benefits flow overwhelmingly to people at the top, while the lost revenue would eventually have to come from everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 14, 2017 and referred to the Ways and Means and Rules committees, which never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess of Texas introduced the Flat Tax Act in the House on February 14, 2017, for himself and Rep. Blake Farenthold [S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, for the supermajority-rule provision, to the Committee on Rules [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the complete action history consists of the introduction and the two referrals [S5].
The bill had only three cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the existing progressive income tax and the estate tax both remained in force, so the largest estates and high-income households are no better off than before, and ordinary taxpayers lost nothing either. The main beneficiary of the outcome is the status quo itself — no revenue was lost and no tax code restructuring occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; the estate tax survived

sides.party_line_note: All four Republicans involved (the sponsor, original co-sponsor, and three cosponsors) were Republicans, and no Democrat supported it, but the bill never advanced far enough for a party-line vote to occur.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes outright, a benefit worth millions only to the largest inheritances, and lets households with mostly investment income elect a flat rate that taxes none of that income. The revenue would otherwise fall on the broader tax base, so the gain for this group comes at the public's expense.

Businesses could elect a 17% tax (19% for two years) on cash-flow income after deducting inputs, wages, and retirement contributions, replacing the corporate income tax. Electing would be beneficial for some firms and costly for others with low deductions, but the option only exists for those who choose it.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and state and local governments as employers
industries.note: Only if they elected into the flat tax — but employers who elect face a new 17-19% tax on the value of noncash employee benefits like health coverage, a cost that would fall on nonprofits and public employers and their budgets.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A flat tax with a large standard deduction and no credits would simplify filing for electors, reducing demand for tax preparation services, but the elective nature means the current complex system remains for everyone who stays in it.
